hints: Focus on what actually has to happen for water to replace the bromine, which bond must break and what role water plays.
Remember that 1-bromopropane is a primary halogenoalkane, so think about whether a carbocation can form easily.
Compare breaking a $\text{C-Cl}$ bond with breaking a $\text{C-Br}$ bond and link bond strength to the rate of hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
**Identify the type of halogenoalkane**

1-bromopropane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, a primary halogenoalkane.

Primary halogenoalkanes react mainly by $S_N2$, where water attacks at the same time as the $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks. No stable carbocation is formed.

**Spot the roles in nucleophilic substitution**

The carbon attached to Br is electron deficient, so it is the electrophile.

Water uses a lone pair on oxygen to attack it, so water is the nucleophile (a weak one, which is why hydrolysis with water alone is slow).

**Decide what controls the rate down Group 17**

The key factor is bond enthalpy, how easily the $\text{C-X}$ bond breaks.

$$\text{C-I} < \text{C-Br} < \text{C-Cl} \text{ in bond strength}$$

So $\text{C-I}$ breaks easiest and reacts fastest, while $\text{C-Cl}$ is strongest and reacts slowest. That makes the statement about 1-chloropropane being slower correct.

options.A: It is true that 1-iodopropane hydrolyses faster, but the reason given is wrong. The $\text{C-Br}$ bond is actually more polar than the $\text{C-I}$ bond because Br is more electronegative than I. Rate is controlled by bond strength, not polarity, and $\text{C-I}$ is weaker so breaks more easily.
options.B: The reaction is slow, but not because water is a weak electrophile. Water is the nucleophile here. The carbon atom is the electrophile. The correct statement is that water is a weak nucleophile.
options.C: A primary halogenoalkane like 1-bromopropane would have to form $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$, a primary carbocation, which is very unstable. The reaction therefore goes by $S_N2$ with no carbocation intermediate.
options.D: The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is shorter and stronger than the $\text{C-Br}$ bond, so it needs more energy to break in the $S_N2$ transition state. 1-chloropropane therefore hydrolyses more slowly than 1-bromopropane. This correctly links bond strength to rate.
